title: Generalized Efficient Quantum Circuit Implementation of Discrete-Time Quantum Walks on Cayley Graphs
abstract: We present a generalized and efficient quantum circuit framework for implementing discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) on Cayley graphs of arbitrary dimension. Building on the Boundary QFT scheme of Razzoli et al., we introduce a systematic multi-stage decomposition of the shift operator for 1D Cayley graphs across three classes of generating sets: inverse-closed without involutions, inverse-closed with an involution, and non-inverse-closed. The decomposition hierarchically factorizes the QFT-diagonalized shift operator into structured block components, progressively reducing the control degree of the required rotation gates and replacing high-degree multi-qubit controlled operations with collections of lower-degree equivalents. We extend this construction to $d$-dimensional torus graphs and provide explicit circuit implementations for an 8-Cayley graph and a $\mathbb{Z}_{16} \times \mathbb{Z}_8$ torus graph as concrete illustrations. Gate complexity analysis using the linear CNOT scaling of Rosa et al. demonstrates that the decomposed implementation achieves a substantial reduction in upper-bound CNOT cost relative to the naive implementation within the regime $k \leq 64$ for inverse-closed graphs and $k \leq 16$ for non-inverse-closed graphs, where $k$ denotes the degree of the generating set. Benchmarking further reveals that this efficiency gain is largely insensitive to the system size $N$, identifying $k$ as the dominant resource parameter for the shift operator. These results provide a scalable and hardware-conscious pathway toward practical DTQW implementations on near-term quantum devices.
summary: This paper presents a generalized, efficient quantum circuit framework for simulating discrete-time quantum walks on arbitrary Cayley graphs. By systematically decomposing the complex shift operator using a multi-stage factorization technique, the authors achieve substantial reductions in required CNOT gates compared to standard methods. This provides a crucial, hardware-conscious tool for realizing quantum walk simulations on near-term quantum hardware.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a generalized and efficient quantum circuit framework for implementing discrete-time quantum walks (DTQWs) on Cayley graphs of arbitrary dimension.
main_result: The proposed multi-stage decomposition of the shift operator significantly reduces the upper-bound CNOT cost compared to naive implementations, providing a scalable pathway for near-term quantum devices.
method: The authors build upon the Boundary QFT scheme by introducing a systematic, hierarchical multi-stage decomposition of the shift operator, which factorizes the QFT-diagonalized operator into structured block components.
model_or_system: The model is the Discrete-Time Quantum Walk (DTQW) evolving on a Cayley graph $\Gamma(G, S)$. The evolution is governed by $U = S(C \otimes I_p)$, where $S$ is the shift operator, which is the primary computational bottleneck.
key_observables: Upper-bound CNOT cost, gate complexity, and the reduction factor compared to naive implementations.
important_parameters: The degree of the generating set ($k$) is identified as the dominant resource parameter, with efficiency gains shown for $k \le 64$ (inverse-closed) and $k \le 16$ (non-inverse-closed).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the linear CNOT scaling established by Rosa et al. and assumes the efficiency gain is largely insensitive to the system size $N$.
figures_summary: The figures illustrate examples of different Cayley graphs and provide a graphical representation of the DTQW setup, including specific optimized quantum circuits for 2D torus graphs.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the DTQW model and the role of the shift operator. It then details the systematic multi-stage decomposition, generalizing the Boundary QFT scheme. The core of the work involves applying this decomposition to specific graph examples (1D and 2D torus graphs) and performing gate complexity analysis to demonstrate the efficiency gains.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the resource estimation for implementing quantum walks, which are fundamental models for quantum search and simulation, making it highly relevant for quantum algorithm development.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Examples of different types of Cayley graphs. (a) An undirected regular graph with an involution at σ = 3. Each edge is color-coded according to its corresponding generator in the generating set. (b) A directed torus grid graph with each cyclic group and its generator edges color-coded accordingly.

Figure 2: Graphical representation of the DTQW setup on an N-node Cayley graph with k generators. Each node represents a position state |x⟩in the Hilbert space H(N) p . The directed edges originating from node 0 illustrate the conditional shifts to neighboring nodes, where each transition is governed by a specific coin state |c⟩from the k-dimensional coin space H(k) c .

Figure 4: Quantum circuit implementation of a single-step discrete-time quantum walk (DTQW) using the decomposed shift operator. The shift operator is realized through a sequence of controlled-NOT operations acting on the position register, with the control provided by the coin register, and an increment operator independent of the coin state. The coin operator is applied prior to the conditional shift, completing one time step of the walk.
Figure 5: Final quantum circuit implementation of a single-step DTQW in the stepwise QFT scheme [20], showing the decomposition of the increment operator using QFT, phase rotations Rλ, and the IQFT.

Figure 6: Quantum circuit implementation of DTQW in the boundary QFT scheme [21]. The QFT and its inverse are implemented only once at the start and the end excluding the SWAP operation. The central block corresponds to the single time step and is to be repeated t times.
